title: South Sikkim for families and seniors
meta_description: Why South Sikkim suits children and older travellers: no permits, low altitude, drives under 2 hours, easy walks, medical help nearby and a calm 5-day plan.
summary: South Sikkim is the gentlest part of the state: the main bases sit at 1,300–2,100 m, no permits are needed for Indian families, children of any age are allowed, and no drive between sights takes more than about 1.5 hours. Pick level sights, rest each afternoon and keep a buffer day for the Siliguri road.

sections.heading: Why the south is the easy half of Sikkim
paras: Many families come to Sikkim wanting snow and lakes and then discover the catch. North Sikkim requires permits, a minimum two-night stay, long days in a vehicle and altitudes above 3,000 m, and children under 5 are not permitted in its protected areas. Nathu La and Tsomgo Lake mean a climb to well over 3,700 m in a single morning. For a toddler, a grandparent with a heart condition or anyone with bad knees, that is a lot to ask.

Namchi district (South Sikkim) is the opposite. Namchi town is at about 1,315 m, Ravangla at about 2,100 m and Temi between 1,200 and 1,800 m, all well below the height where most people feel the altitude. Indian nationals need no permit anywhere on the usual circuit. The sights are big, calm and accessible: two giant statues, a temple complex, a tea garden, monasteries and gardens. And because everything sits on one ridge system, you spend your days seeing things rather than sitting in a car.

sections.heading: Short drives, by the clock
paras: Hill roads average 20 to 25 km an hour, so time matters more than distance. These are realistic times for a private car with stops, in dry weather. The only long drive of the trip is the arrival and departure from Siliguri, and even that is shorter than the run to Gangtok or Pelling.
Break the Siliguri drive at Melli or Jorethang for tea and a toilet stop, and plan to arrive at your hotel before dark, around 5 pm in winter.

sections.heading: Easy walks and level sights
paras: We grade sights for our older guests honestly, by how many steps and slopes they involve. Most South Sikkim sights can be enjoyed with a short walk from the car, and where steps are unavoidable there are places to sit.
list: Buddha Park, Ravangla: wide, almost level paved paths from the gate to the 130 ft statue, lawns and benches; the easiest major sight in Sikkim
Namchi Rock Garden: terraced paths with gentle steps, flowers and a café; take the upper level only if knees are weak
Char Dham, Namchi: large, with many steps between levels; go at 8 am, rest at covered benches, skip the upper platforms if needed
Samdruptse: a short paved path and a few flights of steps from the car park to the Guru Rinpoche statue
Temi Tea Garden: walk downhill along the estate road and have the car meet you below, so there is no climbing back up
Ralang Monastery: the car stops near the courtyard; the main hall has a few steps
Namchi central plaza: level, lit in the evening, with shops and snacks nearby

sections.heading: Children: what works and what to pack
paras: Children usually love Buddha Park's open lawns, the flowers and terraces at the Rock Garden and the sheer size of the Char Dham Shiva. Older children enjoy the tea-plucking at Temi and a short forest walk on the lower part of the Tendong path from Damthang; fit ten-year-olds can manage the full climb to the 2,600 m summit with rests.

The biggest problem for children on hill roads is motion sickness, not altitude. Give a light breakfast, sit them in the middle row facing forward, keep a window open, carry lemon drops or ginger sweets, and ask the driver to stop every hour. Pack warm layers even in May (Ravangla evenings fall to about 10 °C), a rain jacket, sunscreen, a torch for power cuts and any regular medicines. Packaged baby food and nappies are sold in Namchi; in Ravangla the choice is smaller.

sections.heading: Seniors: comfort, health and pace
paras: For travellers over 65, the main points are warmth, pace and access to help. Choose rooms on the ground or first floor, since many hill hotels have stairs and no lift; ask before booking. In winter, ask for a heater or heavy blankets, especially in Ravangla where nights drop near freezing. Plan one main sight in the morning and one gentle one in the afternoon, with a rest after lunch.

Namchi has a district hospital, pharmacies and clinics, so it makes a good base for anyone with ongoing health needs; Ravangla has a primary health centre and pharmacies. Carry prescriptions and enough medicine for the whole trip plus a few days, because specific brands can be hard to find in the hills. If you have heart or lung conditions, check with your doctor, but the altitudes here are moderate.

sections.heading: Food that suits fussy eaters and soft diets
paras: Food is rarely a problem in the south. Every hotel and dhaba serves dal, rice, chapati and a mild vegetable curry, and Namchi has many pure-vegetarian places that cater to pilgrims from the plains, some serving Jain food on request. Momos and thukpa, steamed dumplings and noodle soup, are gentle on the stomach and popular with children. Ask for less chilli: Sikkimese kitchens use the fiery dalle khursani freely, especially in pickles and achar.

For seniors on soft or low-salt diets, tell the hotel kitchen in advance; most will make khichdi, plain soups and boiled vegetables without fuss. Drink boiled or packaged water, carry a refillable bottle and avoid cut fruit from roadside stalls. Milk and curd are easy to find in Namchi. If anyone in your group needs a special diet, mention it when you book a package so the homestays and hotels can plan their shopping, which in the hills is done a day or two ahead.

sections.heading: A gentle five-day plan
paras: This is the shape of our family and senior trips in the south: short days, two bases, no early starts except where the light is worth it, and one free afternoon. It works from either Bagdogra Airport or NJP station.
list: Day 1: Siliguri to Namchi (3.5–4 h), afternoon rest, evening at the central plaza
Day 2: Char Dham at 8 am, lunch, Rock Garden and Samdruptse in the afternoon
Day 3: drive to Ravangla (1 h), Buddha Park after lunch, sunset from the hotel
Day 4: Ralang Monastery and Temi Tea Garden, walking downhill with the car below
Day 5: drive to Bagdogra or NJP (4.5–5 h), leaving after breakfast

sections.heading: When to go and what to avoid
paras: The best months for families and seniors are October to early December (clear, dry, cool) and March to May (mild, flowers, some haze). Winter, December to February, is clear but cold in Ravangla; fine for healthy travellers with warm clothes. Avoid June to September if you can: heavy rain, leeches on paths, and NH10, the main road up the Teesta to Melli, closes after landslides, with long detours via Kalimpong. Check current status before you travel.

Finally, avoid the temptation to add North Sikkim to a trip built for small children or frail seniors. If snow is a must, a day at Tsomgo Lake from Gangtok is a shorter, more controlled outing, and the rest of the trip can stay in the gentle south.

faqs.q: Is South Sikkim good for a family trip with young children?
faqs.a: Yes, it is the easiest part of Sikkim for children. The main bases sit at 1,300–2,100 m, no permits are needed for Indian families, children of any age are allowed (unlike North Sikkim, where under-5s are not permitted in protected areas), and drives between sights are under 1.5 hours. Buddha Park and the Rock Garden are favourites.

faqs.q: Is Ravangla too high for elderly people?
faqs.a: For most healthy seniors, no. Ravangla is about 2,100 m, well below the height where altitude sickness usually begins. The main issue is cold: winter nights are near freezing, so ask for heaters or heavy blankets. Anyone with heart or lung conditions should check with a doctor first.

faqs.q: Which South Sikkim sights have the fewest steps?
faqs.a: Buddha Park at Ravangla is almost level from gate to statue. Namchi's central plaza is level, and the Temi estate road can be walked downhill with the car waiting below. Char Dham has the most steps; go early and rest at the covered benches.

faqs.q: How long is the drive from Bagdogra to Namchi?
faqs.a: About 100 km and 3.5 to 4 hours via Sevoke, the Teesta valley and Melli. Bagdogra Airport is about 15 km from Siliguri, so add half an hour. In the monsoon, landslides on NH10 can force a longer route via Kalimpong; check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Are there hospitals in South Sikkim?
faqs.a: Namchi has a district hospital, pharmacies and private clinics. Ravangla has a primary health centre and pharmacies. For serious emergencies, patients are usually referred to Gangtok or Siliguri. Carry prescriptions and enough medicine for the whole trip plus spare.

faqs.q: How do I stop my child getting carsick on hill roads?
faqs.a: Give a light breakfast, seat the child in the middle row facing forward, keep a window slightly open and ask the driver to stop every hour. Ginger sweets or lemon drops help, and talk to your doctor about motion-sickness medicine before the trip. Short South Sikkim drives make this easier.

faqs.q: What is the best month for seniors to visit South Sikkim?
faqs.a: October and November are the best: dry, clear and cool, with mountain views. March and April are also good, with flowers and mild days. Avoid the monsoon from June to September, and expect cold nights in Ravangla from December to February.

faqs.q: Can we see snow in South Sikkim?
faqs.a: Rarely. Tendong Hill and Maenam sometimes get light snow in January or February, and Ravangla occasionally sees a dusting, but it is not reliable. For guaranteed snow, a day trip to Tsomgo Lake from Gangtok in winter is the gentler option. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Do hotels in Namchi and Ravangla have lifts?
faqs.a: Some newer and larger hotels do; many smaller hill hotels do not, and rooms with views are often up several flights. If stairs are a problem, ask for a ground or first-floor room when you book. Ask us about lift access when we plan a trip for older travellers.
